St. Theodore Stratelates

Saints

St. Theodore Stratelates

St. Theodore the General · St. Theodore of Heraclea

Period
319 in the OCA’s received account
Region
Euchaita; Heraclea in Pontus
Titles / vocation
Martyr · Soldier
Commemoration
February 8

Introduction

St. Theodore Stratelates is the military commander remembered at Heraclea, distinct from St. Theodore the Recruit. The OCA relates his preaching, destruction of idols, severe torture and eventual beheading under Licinius.

Background

[Roman Martyrology on this day. By the modern Greeks on Feb. 8th, but anciently on the 7th. The Acts purport to be written by one Augarius, a notary; he says, “I, the Scribe Augarius, was present, and saw these cruel punishments, and hearing also the pain of his stifled sighs, casting aside my parchments, I threw myself weeping at his feet.” He says also that he wrote this account at the request of the dying martyr. This is almost a certain mark of the hand of a forger—a common expedient. To the account of the martyrdom is prefixed—very probably by a later hand—a story of the fight of S. Theodore with a dragon, which belongs to the Western version of the story of S. George. These Acts certainly existed in their present condition in 550, for they were then translated into Latin.]

Historical1914 account by the Anglican collector Sabine Baring-Gould,volII,February7,printedpp190–191. Its critique of the martyrdom Acts is the historical author’s assessment, not an Orthodox council’s judgment. The app’s commemoration follows the separately identified OCA February8 entry.

[2] Historical reference or published author’s writing · VolII,February7,printedp190,editor’s source note

Life and notable events

S. Theodore of Heraclea, who is not to be confounded with S. Theodore of Amasea, surnamed Tyro, also a warrior martyr, is numbered among the Great Martyrs by the Greek Church.

Theodore of Heraclea was a general of the forces of Licinius, and governor of the country of the Mariandyni, whose capital was Heraclea of Pontus. Here he was sentenced to death by order of the emperor. After having been scourged, and his flesh torn by hooks, and burnt with fire, he was for a short while attached to a cross, and then beheaded.

Historical1914 account by the Anglican collector Sabine Baring-Gould,volII,February7,printedpp190–191. Its critique of the martyrdom Acts is the historical author’s assessment, not an Orthodox council’s judgment. The app’s commemoration follows the separately identified OCA February8 entry.

[2] Historical reference or published author’s writing · VolII,February7,printedp190,biographical paragraphs

The OCA’s longer tradition places his origins in Euchaita and tells of his defeating a destructive serpent before becoming commander at Heraclea. It recounts his breaking the emperor’s gold and silver idols and distributing the pieces to the poor. After surviving torture, he refuses to flee and restrains Christians from taking revenge. The same account includes the opening of prison doors and healings near his final execution. These are features of the received hagiographic narrative, distinguished from independent contemporary documentation.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Euchaita,destruction of idols and final voluntary surrender

Death and martyrdom

In the OCA account he is healed after crucifixion, then later beheaded. The failed crucifixion therefore must not be mistaken for the final death method. The received life gives February 8, 319 as the day of execution.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Crucifixion, healing and final execution

Writings and legacy

Relics at S. Saviour’s, Venice. S. Theodore is regarded as one of the chief patrons of the Venetian republic. The body of this glorious martyr was brought from Constantinople to Venice by Mark Dandolo, in 1260.

In Art, S. Theodore appears as a warrior in armour, very generally trampling on the dragon. He is to be distinguished from S. George by being represented on foot, whereas S. George usually appears mounted.

Historical1914 account by the Anglican collector Sabine Baring-Gould,volII,February7,printedpp190–191. Its critique of the martyrdom Acts is the historical author’s assessment, not an Orthodox council’s judgment. The app’s commemoration follows the separately identified OCA February8 entry.

[2] Historical reference or published author’s writing · VolII,February7,printedpp190–191,relics and art
